title: How Educators Get Addicted to Heroin
author: Matt Spivey
summary: Matt Spivey uses a deliberately provocative title to borrow a lesson from Eric Ries's book Incorruptible. At its center is Costco's $1.50 hot dog, whose price CEO Jim Sinegal refused to raise, comparing small price increases to heroin: you take a little and want a little more. Spivey argues that the same addiction to small, rationalized compromises has hollowed out universities, and he lists what he personally witnessed, including annual tuition hikes, a president's raise amid faculty pay freezes, pressure to lower grading standards, cheaper but weaker online courses, and lowered admissions standards. He extends the critique to K-12, from social promotion of nonreaders to repeated warnings instead of consequences. Invoking Rick Rubin's refusal to consider near-term incentives, he calls for schools to adopt a 'forever mindset' and to decide which principles they will not bend. The piece ends by insisting that trust with students and families is the asset institutions cannot afford to spend.
points: Sinegal kept the Costco hot dog at $1.50 because it symbolized a promise to customers, even as a Big Mac rose to $7.
Spivey frames tuition hikes, grade leniency, weaker online courses, and lowered admissions as small 'hits' that each seem harmless.
He recounts an administrator admitting that online courses taught students less but were kept because they made money.
K-12 has its own version, including passing students who cannot read and repeated warnings instead of consequences.
Institutions should identify the values that cost them in the short term but sustain them in the long term.
quotes: Sinegal has said that increasing the price of a store product by just $0.03 could add a 50% increase in income, and no one would even notice. It’s so easy, which is why everyone does it. But it’s the “little bit more” that’s so addictive.
This disregard for trust, caused by a pattern of addictive behaviors, is what has led to the diminishment of universities in the twenty-first century.

Just a small tuition increase. Just a slight raise for the school president. Just a little more leniency in how we grade. Just a few more unqualified students admitted. Just a couple of additional online classes to replace in-person learning.

I sat in a meeting with the same leader where he openly acknowledged that instruction was poorer and students learned less in online courses, but they were cheaper than in-person courses, so they were a way for the school to make more money.
This type of thinking isn’t unique to higher education—K-12 has its own version as well. Just one more student passed on to 4th grade who can’t read or do arithmetic.
Because it’s all short-term thinking. It’s all a choice to take the path of least resistance to get to more. More money, more students, more status.
What have universities decided to hold to, the principles on which they refuse to bend? What are the values that may cost them in the short term but will sustain them in the long term?
Universities must remember to build and maintain trust with students and families. Otherwise, they might be soon out of business.
